title: POC Weekly Sync - Quality Eval & Guardrails
customer_attendees: Dr. Emily Ross - Head of Product
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality eval results, discuss prompt-set regressions, adjust scoring/guardrails, and agree next steps for benchmarking and security artifacts.
topics: Deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-30 14:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Dr. Emily Ross (Haven), Kevin Liu (Haven), Sara Patel (Haven)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, really quick — we'll go through the eval spreadsheet, hit the regressions you flagged, and then talk guardrails & next steps.
[00:28] Dr. Emily Ross: Sounds good. Sorry, had a late morning. We got the report, thanks. Quick context — objective this week was to see whether the new prompt templates reduce hallucinations on clinical FAQ answers.
[00:46] Daniel Park: Great, and we're looking at the same testset you sent last week, right? 400 prompts, mixed short/long, and the pass/fail is the domain-accuracy rubric you shared?
[01:05] Kevin Liu: Yes, same set. We also added the new negation/edge-case prompts; those were the ones that tripped the model last time.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Okay cool. Quick note — some transcriber weirdness in the spreadsheet, you might see "K-V cash" instead of KV cache, and "Redwood Dedicate" in a couple of notes, but that's just the auto captions.
[01:38] Daniel Park: Right, so summary first: baseline model (open-llm-v2) on hosted had overall accuracy 86%, hallucination rate 9%, and a regression on the drug-interaction prompts — those dropped from 92% to 78% after the prompt template change.
[02:05] Dr. Emily Ross: Oof, the drop on drug interaction is the big one for us. Any idea why?
[02:18] Daniel Park: Initial hypothesis — the guardrail we added to enforce brevity made the model omit conditionals. So it answered shorter but lost nuance, which in drug interactions is critical.
[02:33] Kevin Liu: We noticed that in the examples — the model truncates the conditional clauses. Could be an instruction-following tradeoff with length-limited prompts.
[02:49] Maya Chen: We can tune the prompt scoring weight to preference completeness over brevity for those patterns. Also Daniel, remind them about our "quality profiles" in the console — you can make per-route scoring thresholds.
[03:07] Daniel Park: Yes, in Redwood Console you can set a quality profile that changes the temperature, max tokens, and the guardrail enforcement for specific prompt tags. We can bump the temperature down or up depending on desired conservatism, but for safety-critical drug answers I'd recommend stricter grounding and a higher hallucination penalty.
[03:30] Sara Patel: When you say "grounding" — do you mean retrieving from our knowledge base? We need to ensure any source citations are included for audit.
[03:42] Daniel Park: Exactly. Use the retrieval-augmented generation route; include source citations and a minimum confidence threshold. That way the model will reply with "can't answer" or cite sources when confidence is low.
[03:56] Dr. Emily Ross: On the audit point, we'll need retention settings and logs for any patient-proximal queries. Sara, do you have the SOC 2 / data retention requirements?
[04:10] Sara Patel: Yes — 7 years retention for certain logs, SSO via SAML is required, and we need customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for private deployments. We asked for the security pack last week but haven't seen the detailed KMS flow.
[04:28] Maya Chen: We'll share the full security artifact — SOC 2 type II report, network diagrams for private deployment, and the KMS integration doc. Daniel, I'll follow up with the private deployment checklist.
[04:43] Daniel Park: I also want to call out that in Dedicated mode you can opt into disk-level encryption and customer-supplied keys; on Private we support on-prem HSM flows. There might be some network setup time for your infra team.
[04:59] Kevin Liu: Good to know. For the regression — is it easier to revert to the old prompt template for the drug-interaction route while we iterate?
[05:12] Daniel Park: Yes, you can do a canary rollback per-route in the console, and run A/B with the new template on a small % of traffic. That should give quick signals.
[05:24] Dr. Emily Ross: How long to get the adjusted prompts and re-run the tests? We have a compliance checkpoint next Tuesday.
[05:34] Maya Chen: We can push a prompt update today and re-run the eval overnight if you give us access to the scoring harness, or we can run it and share results by Friday.
[05:46] Kevin Liu: Please run it and share — we want to see a before/after. Also include the per-prompt failure cases.
[05:56] Daniel Park: Noted. On scoring — we used a blended metric: exact-match domain accuracy (70% weight), hallucination penalty (20%), and style/adherence metrics (10%). We can adjust weights if you prefer more emphasis on recall.
[06:12] Dr. Emily Ross: For our use case, precision is higher priority but we can't sacrifice recall completely. So keep accuracy priority but penalize hallucinations heavily.
[06:24] Maya Chen: We'll flip the weights to accuracy 60 / hallucination 35 / style 5 in the next run and show both.
[06:33] Sara Patel: A couple security questions — does Redwood do PII redaction automatically before logs are stored? We want to avoid PHI in any long-term logs unless it's explicitly needed.
[06:45] Daniel Park: There's a redaction pipeline — we can scrubbing at ingest and only store hashed metadata. For customers on Private, you can choose to disable log export to the control plane entirely.
[06:57] Kevin Liu: Perfect. Also, on model variants — could a smaller quantized model reduce hallucinations for our domain?
[07:08] Daniel Park: Sometimes smaller models hallucinate more, but quantized variants can reduce latency/cost. We recommend testing a vetted variant from our catalog; Redwood-verified profiles show expected tradeoffs. We'll include a candidate variant list.
[07:25] Dr. Emily Ross: Any cost delta we should expect for dedicated vs hosted for our expected qps?
[07:34] Maya Chen: For your pilot volume, hosted is cheaper short-term, Dedicated becomes cost-effective at sustained throughput. We'll send a cost projection for your workload.
[07:45] Kevin Liu: Back to the regression — examples we attached show contradictory answers on dosing intervals. Could that be from the KB retrieval returning multiple sources?
[07:57] Daniel Park: Yes, if the retrieval returns conflicting sources and you don't have a ranking/lens step, the model might synthesize incorrectly. We can add a source selection or canonicalization pass in the pipeline.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Quick aside — we saw one false positive where the model invented a citation. We'll add a guardrail that requires inline source tokens for any clinical claim, otherwise respond with a fallback "needs human review".
[08:29] Dr. Emily Ross: That's good. How do we tune that threshold? The scoring harness can mark any response without citation as fail?
[08:38] Daniel Park: Yes, tag the prompt route as "citation_required" and the quality profile will auto-fail responses without citations above a certain confidence.
[08:49] Kevin Liu: Implementation detail — for the leash/guardrail, do we inject additional system tokens or use post-hoc validation?
[08:58] Daniel Park: We recommend both: inject a system instruction to prefer grounded answers and add a post-hoc validation step that checks for source tokens. It's a belt-and-suspenders approach.
[09:11] Maya Chen: Okay, next, timeline and outputs — we'll run two evals (current weights vs adjusted weights), produce a regression diff, and flag per-prompt fixes. We'll also produce a short doc on guardrail design patterns for clinical QA.
[09:27] Dr. Emily Ross: Sounds actionable. For the compliance checkpoint — can we get the security pack and the KMS flow by Monday?
[09:36] Sara Patel: Monday would be ideal.
[09:39] Maya Chen: We'll prioritize that.
[09:43] Daniel Park: One more note — we saw one example where tokenization differences caused the model to drop a trailing clause. Might be sequence-length truncation or EOS handling; I'll log a ticket to investigate runtime kernel behavior for that model.
[09:58] Kevin Liu: Appreciate it.
[10:02] Dr. Emily Ross: Okay let's talk next steps and ownership.
[10:08] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to run adjusted evals and share results by Friday; Redwood to send security pack and KMS doc by Monday; Haven to provide access to their scoring harness or give CI keys; schedule a short follow-up on Friday to review results.
[10:26] Kevin Liu: We'll grant CI keys today.
[10:30] Sara Patel: I'll review the security docs when they come and ping if anything missing.
[10:36] Maya Chen: Great. Any other questions?
[10:40] Dr. Emily Ross: None from me. Thanks everyone.
[10:44] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links and the updated spreadsheet. Bye.

End of transcript. Some transcriber errors probable (names and product words).
